question: If app/layout.tsx defines `title: { default: 'Constela', template: '%s | Constela' }` and app/blog/page.tsx omits the `title` field, what <title> does Next.js render?
options: An empty <title> tag
| Constela
Constela
undefined | Constela
explanation: When a child page omits `title`, Next.js uses the parent layout's `title.default` value ('Constela') without applying the `%s` template.

question: Why can both generateMetadata() and Page() call the same data-fetching function without doubling database or fetch work in Next.js?
options: Next.js runs generateMetadata only in the browser after hydration
Request memoization deduplicates identical GET fetch() and React cache() calls within the same server render pass
generateMetadata runs once per year at domain registration
Page() receives the raw HTML returned by generateMetadata()
explanation: Next.js memoizes identical GET fetch() calls and React cache()-wrapped reads across generateMetadata and the Server Component page in the same request.

question: What does app/sitemap.ts export to generate /sitemap.xml automatically?
options: A React component rendering raw <urlset> JSX tags
A default function returning an array of typed MetadataRoute.Sitemap entries ({ url, lastModified, changeFrequency, priority })
A CSS stylesheet containing canonical URLs
A NextResponse redirect to Google Search Console
explanation: app/sitemap.ts exports a default function returning an array of MetadataRoute.Sitemap objects that Next.js serializes into valid XML at /sitemap.xml.

question: What is the primary purpose of app/robots.ts in a Next.js App Router application?
options: To authenticate user sessions before middleware runs
To compress PNG images before they are uploaded
To configure automated browser unit tests
To declare crawler allow/disallow rules and link search engines to your sitemap.xml endpoint
explanation: app/robots.ts generates /robots.txt with structured user-agent allow/disallow rules and the canonical sitemap URL for search engine crawlers.

question: A layout defines openGraph with siteName and images. A child page defines openGraph: { title: "Post" }. What happens to the parent fields?
options: They are automatically deep-merged into the child object
They are lost unless the child explicitly preserves them, for example by spreading shared values or reading parent metadata in generateMetadata
Next.js rejects the child metadata
They become top-level metadata fields
explanation: Metadata is shallowly merged across segments: a child openGraph object replaces the parent object entirely. Explicitly copy shared fields to retain them.
